choices: Avoir or être in the imperfect, plus the past participle
Avoir or être in the present, plus the past participle
The imperfect stem, plus the future endings
Two past participles in a row
questions.why: It is the passé composé with the auxiliary shifted into the imperfect: j'ai mangé → j'avais mangé. Nothing else about the tense changes.

questions.q: How do auxiliary choice and participle agreement work in the plus-que-parfait?
choices: Everything takes avoir, and nothing agrees
Everything takes être, and everything agrees with the subject
Exactly as in the passé composé
The participle agrees with the object, always
questions.why: The only change from the passé composé is the tense of the auxiliary. If you can build je suis allé, you can build j'étais allé.
Finir takes avoir, and the imperfect of avoir for nous is avions. The participle stays flat: fini.
Aller takes être, so the participle agrees with the feminine singular subject: allée. Auxiliary in the imperfect: était.
Naître is on the être list and its participle is né, so feminine plural gives nées.
Reflexives take être, and here se is the direct object, so the participle agrees with the subject: levé. The reflexive pronoun sits before the auxiliary.

questions.q: « Quand je suis arrivé, il ___ (partir) déjà. »
questions.why: My arrival is the past point; his leaving is earlier still, so plus-que-parfait. Déjà slots between the auxiliary and the participle, as pas and encore do.

questions.q: Report it: « J'ai mangé. » → Il a dit qu'il ___
questions.why: Reported speech pushes each tense one step back, so a passé composé in the original becomes a plus-que-parfait in the report.

questions.q: Report it: « Je suis partie tôt. » → Elle a dit qu'elle ___ tôt.
questions.why: Partir takes être, so the participle keeps agreeing with the feminine subject even after the shift: était partie.

questions.q: Which of these is the notorious error?
choices: Si j'avais su, je serais venu
Si j'aurais su, je serais venu
Il était fatigué parce qu'il n'avait pas dormi
questions.why: Si never takes a conditional. The si half gets the pluperfect, and the conditional goes in the other half: si j'avais su, je serais venu.

questions.q: Build the sentence: He was tired because he hadn't slept.
questions.why: The imperfect states the past situation, the pluperfect explains what came before it. The negation wraps the auxiliary, as always.
Être in the imperfect plus parti, the standard shape of an earlier past. Déjà is the word that most often flags it.

questions.q: In a past narrative, which tense carries the events themselves, in order?
questions.why: Passé composé for the events, imparfait for the circumstances around them, plus-que-parfait for anything already finished before the story's present moment.

questions.q: Say this out loud: if only I had known!
questions.why: Si seulement plus the pluperfect is the fixed way of expressing regret about the past.

questions.q: Give the four main uses of the plus-que-parfait, with a short French example each.
a: 1. An earlier past: Quand je suis arrivé, il était déjà parti. 2. Explaining a past situation: Il était fatigué parce qu'il n'avait pas dormi. 3. Regret with si seulement: Si seulement j'avais su ! 4. The si half of the past unreal condition: Si j'avais su, je serais venu. Plus reported speech, where a passé composé shifts back to it: Il a dit qu'il avait mangé.
questions.why: All of them are the same idea seen from different angles: a point in the past, and something already complete before it.
